title: No homomorphisms between split tori and abelian varieties
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], let $A/k$ be an abelian variety [def-sc-abelian-variety], and let $T=\mathbf G_m^r$ for an integer $r\geq0$ [def-sc-gm-ga]. Every $k$-group-scheme homomorphism $T\to A$ is the zero homomorphism, and every $k$-group-scheme homomorphism $A\to T$ is the zero homomorphism [def-sc-group-scheme]. Here the zero homomorphism is the structure map to $\operatorname{Spec}k$ followed by the identity section of the target. Equivalently both $\operatorname{Hom}_{k\text{-grp}}(T,A)$ and $\operatorname{Hom}_{k\text{-grp}}(A,T)$ are trivial groups.

source.place: Proposition 8.1(b) and Example 8.4, printed p.149, for affine smooth connected images in an abelian variety; §8(e), printed p.151, for the absence of homomorphisms from complete connected group varieties to affine groups. Apply the homomorphism image factorization of Theorem 5.39, printed pp.108–109.

proof.text: Write $p_X:X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ for a structure map and $e_X$ for a group identity section. By the definition of $\mathbf G_m$ and repeated use of the affine fibre-product formula, $T=\operatorname{Spec}k[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_r^{\pm1}]$ is an affine finite-type group scheme. It is a torus under the definition in lem-sfb-multiplicative-type-largest-subtorus, whose statement gives smoothness and connectedness. For $r=0$ the coordinate algebra is $k$ and these assertions still hold. Being affine, $T$ is separated over $k$ by lem-weil-pbc-affine-source-morphism-separated. By def-sc-abelian-variety, $A$ is proper, smooth and connected; in particular it is separated and of finite type.

source.place: Proposition 8.1(b), Example 8.4, printed p.149; Section 8(e), printed p.151; Theorem 5.39, printed p.108.

proof.text: Let $f:T\to A$ be a homomorphism. Apply the homomorphism theorem to obtain $T\xrightarrow{q}I\xrightarrow{i}A$ with $i$ a closed immersion, $f=i\circ q$, and $I=T/N$ as an fppf quotient, where $N=\ker f$ is a closed normal finite-type subgroup. The closed immersion $N\hookrightarrow T$ is an affine morphism by def-weil-closed-immersion, so $N$ is affine because $T$ is, by lem-weil-pbc-affine-morphism-permanence(2). Thus the affine normal quotient theorem applies to $N\subseteq T$: its representing quotient is affine and smooth. It is geometrically connected because $k$ is already algebraically closed and $T$ is connected. The two quotient representations are canonically isomorphic compatibly with $q$, so these properties hold for $I$. No assertion that $N$ itself is smooth is used.

source.place: Proposition 8.1(b), Example 8.4, printed p.149; Section 8(e), printed p.151; Theorem 5.39, printed p.108.

proof.text: The closed immersion $i:I\hookrightarrow A$ makes $I$ proper over $k$ by lem-weil-pbc-closed-immersion-proper(c). Since $I$ is smooth over a field it is reduced by sbc-lem-smooth-geometrically-reduced. The constant-global-sections theorem now applies: $I$ is nonempty (it has its identity section), proper, reduced and connected, and $k$ is algebraically closed. Its set of connected components is a singleton, so the structural map $k\to\Gamma(I,\mathcal O_I)$ is an isomorphism.

source.place: Proposition 8.1(b), Example 8.4, printed p.149; Section 8(e), printed p.151; Theorem 5.39, printed p.108.

proof.text: Because $I$ is affine, apply the affine-target bijection to the maps $1_I$ and $e_I\circ p_I:I\to I$. Their maps on global sections agree: the structure map identifies $\Gamma(I,\mathcal O_I)$ with $k$, and every $k$-algebra endomorphism of $k$ is the identity. Thus $1_I=e_I\circ p_I$. Substituting into the factorization gives $f=i\circ e_I\circ p_I\circ q=e_A\circ p_T$, since $i$ preserves identity sections and $q$ is over $k$. This is equality of scheme morphisms, not just equality on $k$-points.

source.place: Proposition 8.1(b), Example 8.4, printed p.149; Section 8(e), printed p.151; Theorem 5.39, printed p.108.

proof.text: For a homomorphism $g:A\to T$, smoothness of $A$ gives reducedness by sbc-lem-smooth-geometrically-reduced. Properness, connectedness and the identity section of $A$ give $\Gamma(A,\mathcal O_A)=k$ via the constant-global-sections theorem. The affine-target bijection, applied to affine $T$, therefore expresses $g$ as $c\circ p_A$ for a $k$-point $c:\operatorname{Spec}k\to T$: its section map is the composite $\Gamma(T,\mathcal O_T)\xrightarrow{c^\sharp}k\to\Gamma(A,\mathcal O_A)$. Composing with $e_A$ gives $c=g\circ e_A=e_T$, because $g$ is a group homomorphism and $p_A\circ e_A=1$. Hence $g=e_T\circ p_A$, the zero homomorphism. Both Hom groups therefore contain just their zero element.

source.place: Proposition 8.1(b), Example 8.4, printed p.149; Section 8(e), printed p.151; Theorem 5.39, printed p.108.
